comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> The Janissaries were an elite corps in the service of the Ottoman Empire. They were composed of war captives and Christian youths, converted to Islam, pressed into service, and trained under the strictest discipline."

The soldiers were grouped in massed formations to maximize the firepower of the relatively short-ranged weapons and for easier control of the formation on the field of battle. As a general rule, most armies of the time used a "battleline" composed of two ra..."

title: Ship of the Line (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> The Napoleonic Era encompassed the "Age of Sail," a time when mighty Ships of the Line tore into one another with rows upon rows of guns: ball shot, grape shot, chain shot, a pull to stern and fire! Rake the enemy ship and throw grappling hooks. And then the desperate hand-to-hand on the rocking, creaking decks, as men armed with sabres and [pistolas] wavered back and forth in a fight to the death."

title: Troop Transport (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> This represents a lightly armed sailing vessel capable of transporting quantities of troops for military purposes. Such ships were used well into the 1800s until supplanted by wooden (and later iron-clad) steamships."

title: Soldado (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> "Soldado" means soldier, and although Spanish infantry during the Napoleonic Era was not considered excellent by most accounts, when it came time to wage a war of resistance in 1808, the Spanish Soldado proved that national pride and pluck has its virtues."

title: Sekhan (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> The Sekhan Ottoman infantry were semi-permanent troops raised by provincial governors. While some Sekhan units were well-trained and highly skilled in battle (almost the equal of the Jannisseries), most were actually poorly trained."

title: Jaeger (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> "Jaeger" is a Prussian name for a hunter. In the Prussian army, elite light infantry were typically recruited among professional foresters and game wardens. The term was used by other nationalites as well, like the Russians, whose Jaeger infantry were decent soldiers, good on both the attack and on the defense."

title: Redcoat (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> British infantry of the Napoleonic era was famed for its red uniforms, a color that not only was easily recognizable on the battlefield, but also represented the power and quality of the men who wore them. British redcoat infantry were excellent on the attack and defense."

title: Voltigeur (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> The French Voltigeur were light infantry, well-trained, often elite, with a very high morale. The Voltigeur were excellent on the attack and just as formidible holding a line."

title: Imperial Guard (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Protected "[[Imperial Guard (Civ3)/Civilopedia]]" ([Edit=Allow only administrators] (indefinite) [Move=Allow only administrators] (indefinite))

title: Imperial Guard (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> Every army during the Napoleonic Era had its elite forces. For the French, the Imperial Guard were the pride of the battlefield. Credited with winning many battles, French elite infantry -- the "Old Guard", "Middle Guard" and "Young Guard" -- was comprised of seasoned veterans that could be relied upon to carry the day."

title: Lifeguard (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> Every army during the Napoleonic Era had its elite forces. For the British, the soldiers of the Lifeguard were well-trained and excellent fighters, dedicated to preserving the honor and power of the British Empire."

title: Guard (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> Every army during the Napoleonic Era had its elite forces. For the Russians, the Guard Grenadier battalions were excellent soldiers, stalwart, hearty veterans capable of both a valiant attack or a stout defense."

title: Grenzer (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> Grenzers were Austrian light infantry originally mustered in Croatia. Grenzers were promised a land entitlement in return for protecting border ("Grenze") areas against the Turks. Battalions of "Grenzinfanterie" were used as skirmishers, but they often fought in closed order."

title: Grand Battery (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> A "Grand Battery", as used by the French at Waterloo, comprised hundreds of guns, frequently with orders to concentrate their fire on one unit or location. The shock and disruption of a carefully planned and executed grand battery attack could turn the tide of battle, and indeed helped Napoleon win many of his battles. The Grand Battery is far superior to the normal cannon battery unit."

title: Fusilier (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> The first Prussian Fusilier units were comprised of artillery-trained soldiers armed with flintlock "fusils" that did not need a burning match, thus reducing the danger of accidental powder explosions. Fusiliers were converted into regular line infantry when the flintlock musket became standard issue. In the Prussian army, Fusiliers were often considered second-rate soldiers, culled from the youngest and least tra..."

title: Imperial Cavalry (Civ3)/Civilopedia

Proud and powerful heavily armored cuirassiers, carabiniers and Garde Grenadiers a Cheval, redefined the cavalry charge, and instilled fear in the hearts of all who faced them."

These heavy cavalry units were used sparingly during the early years of the Napoleonic wars, but came to prominence after 1812 (and especially at the Battle of Waterloo). These heavy units were used as "shoc..."

title: Cuirassier (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> "Cuirass" refers to a type of torso armor consisting of a back and breast plate. Prussian Cuirassiers were valiant cavalry soldiers, equally strong on both the attack and on the defense."

title: Palace of the Masks (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> The Palace of the Masks is one of the splendors of Mesoamerica. Located in the Mayan city of Kabah, it's adorned with over 250 rain-god masks inlaid across six separate tiers. Each mask comprises 30 pieces of mosaic stone, all brilliantly sculpted by Mayan craftsman. At its rear rests several large warrior sculptures. Archeologists believe that the palace once served as terminus for a roadway connected Kabah to Ux..."

title: Caracol Observatory (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> The Caracol Observatory is located in the Mayan city of Chichen Itza. Like a modern-day observatory, Caracol has a spiral staircase leading up to the top of a stone dome where a small room looks out onto the sky. From this room, Mayan kings and priests could hold rituals and observe the stars. A small western window in the room shows the setting sun on March 21 (the vernal equinox)."

comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> The royal tomb of the Lord of Sipan is a testament to the wealth and ingenuity of the ancient Moche culture of Peru. Regaled splendidly in the clothing of his office, Lord Sipan was about 40-ish at the time of death, and it’s believed that he ruled as a divine god-king of the Moche world."

title: Temple of the Moon (Civ3)/Mesoamerica/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> The Andean peoples who lived in the hot, humid lowlands feared the relentless heat of the sun. Their worship thus turned to the moon. The Incan Temple of the Moon sat upon the (appropriately named) Island of the Moon, and served as a acclahausi (or home) for the so-called "Chosen Women" of the moon god. Unlike other Incan buildings, its walls were covered with dried mud painted yellow and red."

Lord Pacal had descended to the Pal..."

title: Tezcatlipoca's War Rage (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> Tezcatlipoca, also known as the “smoked mirror”, was a prominent god in Toltec society. His nature was warlike and tyrannical, and legend has it that Ce Acatl Topiltzin, the greatest Toltec ruler and priest of Quetzalcoatl, was driven from the city of Tula by followers of Tezcatlipoca. Topiltzin and his followers fled south, where they eventually captured the Mayan city of Chichen Itza."

title: Palace of the Inca (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> On a small island in Lake Titicaca (called the Island of the Sun) sits the Palace of the Inca. This small 52 foot by 46 foot structure is believed to mark the birthplace of the first Incas. In its day, the palace contained fabulous wealth, and it's likely that the Incan king (the Sapa-Inca) made an annual pilgramage to it to worship and give thanks to the sun for creating his children... the Inca."

comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> The Amazon Jungle is an ecological wonder, a treasure trove of exotic animals, plants, and mysterious tribes. title: Jade (Civ3)/Mesoamerica/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> Jade was a vital resource for the Mesoamericans. Primarily mined from quarries in Guatemala, its color varied from dark green to light blue-green and even gray. Jade was prized for its beauty and for its ritual uses. Tombs of important people, rulers, nobles, etc. were often packed with large quantities of this mineral. It was also Used in jewelry, figurines, and mosaics, and as inlays in stone and shells. Wealthy..."

title: Stone Quarry (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> Without stone quarries, Mesoamerican culture could not have thrived, and stone carvers were vital to the culture. Enormous blocks of limestone and granite were culled from the earth by driving wedges into the rock face until pieces split away. Thousands of workers were used to haul these stones to the work sites."

title: Exotic Birds (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> Mesoamericans used a variety of different bird feathers as a currency and for their headdresses and costumes. The most commonly used feathers were from the Quetzal bird, found in the Guatemalan highlands. Quetzalcoatl, the feathered serpent, legendary god-king for the Aztecs and the Mayas (who called him Kukulcan) shares his name with this bird."

title: Llamas (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> Llamas were (and still are) very important to Andean culture. The Incas used llamas to portage goods across the steep Andes Mountains, and used their course wool to make sacks and rope. Llamas were also a meat source, and were sacrificed to the gods during religious ceremonies."

title: Maize (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> It's believed that around 5000 BC, the first Mesoamericans learned to grow maize (or corn) in and around the highlands of Guatemala and central Mexico. Once the practice became commonplace, maize changed the cultures of Mexico and Central America forever.   A Mayan cornfield was called a [milpa]. title: Salt (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> Salt was a major trade good in Mesoamerica and a very important part of the Mayan diet. Salt was also used medicinally and in religious ceremonies."

comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> The Cacao plant (or Coca plant) was the source of cocoa and chocolate. title: Tambo (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> Tambos were buildings strategically spaced out along the Incas' imperial road system. Used as way stations, travelers could stop and rest at these sites, and also barter trade goods and participate in cultural events. With their tambos, their llamas, and their Chasqui scouts, the Incan empire was able to spread their cultural, political, and military influence throughout the Andes Mountains."

title: Stela (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> Many Mesoamerican societies celebrated important religious events by building stone stelae. These stone carvings were often inscribed with the event’s date, and described the occasion with hieroglyphics letters and numbers. One of the most beautifully wrought stelae (called Stela H) was constructed in the Mayan city of Copan in 782 A.D. This wonderfully conceived stela shows a Mayan king in full ceremonial garb."

title: Sacrificial Altar (Civ3)/Mesoamerica/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> Sacrificial altars were commonplace in Mesoamerican cities. They were often made of granite or limestone, and placed atop a prominent temple overlooking the city plaza. The likenesses of gods or murals of great battles were carved into their surfaces, and when a sacrifice was made, the blood from the slain flowed into the crevices and onto the floor."

comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> The Aztec king Netzahualcoyotl is credited with devising the strict, yet highly effective, Aztec legal system. His simple crime-preventive philosophy called for the strangulation of thieves and the clubbing death of dissident lords. He also advocated strangulation and/or burning of adulterers."

Fish from Lake Titicaca and the numerous streams and rivers, and the vast coastlines of the Pacific Ocean and the Gulf of Mexico, provided a limitless supply of fresh meat."

This great ball court measured 274 feet by 120 feet and was marked by rings 4 feet in diameter and 20 feet off the ground."

title: Enslavement (advance) (Civ3)/Mesoamerica/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> Slaves were an integral part of Mesoamerican society. Slaves were obtained, primarily, through warfare. For the Maya, the acquisition of slaves through battle was a primary reason for war. Slaves were used as cheap laborers and for ritual sacrifice to the gods. Some of the most powerful and prestigious people in Aztec society were the [tlaltlani] (or “bathers of slaves”) slave traders."

title: Stone Carving (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> A key artistic and cultural skill in Mesoamerican society was stone carving. Without it, the majestic temples of Tikal, the glorious and mysterious walls of Machu Picchu, and the wondrous monuments of Tenochtitlan could not have been conceived. For centuries, artisans toiled over blocks of granite great and small, and forged a body of masonry that stands, to this day, as a testament to the ingenuity of ancient man."

comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> Exotic costumery and body augmentation were important aspects of Mesoamerican culture, particularly for the nobility classes. Golden earrings and nose rings were common, and Mayan leaders, in their pursuit to “become” the jaguar, would sharpen their teeth to fine points and tattoo their faces with spots."

Rich soil is placed inside each terrace section, and stonewalls dividing each terrace support the soil and keep it from eroding away from rain or wind."

comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> The Mesoamericans were great sports fans, and they loved their ball games. title: Sacking (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> A barbarian nation with the Sacking advance has achieved its greatest military strength. No city in the Roman Empire or other barbarian tribe is safe. The barbarians are now in a position to wipe out a portion of the empire for good and establish their rule over the formerly Roman lands."

title: Pillaging (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> Barbarians who have achieved the Pillaging advance are now a threat to the very foundations of the Roman empire. Roman towns are now in danger of being overrun, and even the capital at Rome could be quickly seized if the Romans are not careful. Of course, just this fate did befall the Roman capital in 410 AD."

title: Warlord (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> The warlord is the fourth and highest level of barbarian in Fall of Rome. They represent the pinnacle of barbarian power as symbolized by Attila's army of Huns that terrorized Europe at the time of the battle of Chalons in 451 AD. Warlords strike terror into the hearts of citizens and soldiers alike and do not hesitate to burn and sack anything in their path."

title: Pillager (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> The pillager is the third level of barbarian in Fall of Rome. They represent the barbarians of the early 5th Century, epitomized by the Visigoths under Alaric who sacked Rome in 410 AD. The barbarians of this period had reached a new level of ambition and daring. They did not hesitate to move directly against the greatest symbol of Roman power and prestige to force the Romans into paying tribute."

title: Raider (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> The raider is the initial level of barbarian in Fall of Rome. They represent the early units that harrassed the fringes of the Roman Empire in the 4th Century without causing major disruptions.  A good historical example of raiders are the Angle, Saxon, and Jute tribesmen that harrassed the eastern shore of Britain and forced the Romans to build the Saxon Shore fortifications along that sea coast."

title: Marauder (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> The marauder is the second level of barbarian in Fall of Rome. They represent the increased level of barbarian activity after 370 AD, the year that the Huns swept into Europe from the steppes and forced the Germanic barbarians to move west against Rome. The most decisive battle of this period was the Visigoth defeat of the Eastern Emperor Valens at Adrianople in 378 AD."

title: Migrant (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> The barbarian nations of this period had few large settlements and were equipped to quickly pick up and resettle in a new area. The Visigoths moved from the Balkans to Rome, sacking it in 410, before settling in southern Gaul.  They would then displace the Vandals from Spain. The Vandal migration was the most dramatic, for they left their home in Eastern Europe and migrated to Spain, then to North Africa, and fina..."

title: Church (Civ3)/Mesopotamia/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> The church represents the place of worship for a $LINK<monotheistic=TECH_Monotheism> religion, the belief in one Supreme Being. It is accepted by many that the Judeans were the first to practice a truly monotheistic religion, perhaps as early as the sixth century BC."

title: Burial Mound (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> Since prehistoric times man has used burial mounds of varying proportions and construction to inter the final remains of vaunted leaders. In fact, according to some anthropologists, one of the first true signs of the human imagination at work is the burial mound, as it provides the first evidence of man’s becoming aware of the possible existence of an afterlife."

title: City Park (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> Even in ancient times city planners realized that it was wise to reserve certain areas of cities for recreation and relaxation. Archeological evidence from many ancient cities, such as Nineveh and Babylon, indicate that parks, frequently located near important temples, were an important part of most ancient Mesopotamian cities."

comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> The art of storytelling eventually led to drama as a form of entertainment for the masses. The rise of drama eventually necessitated a structure in which to conduct public performances, thus was born the amphitheatre. The ancient amphitheatre was typically a semi-circular or elliptical structure in which a central stage was surrounded by rising tiers of seats. Earliest forms would commonly have been carved directl..."

Thus arose the need for semi-permanent housing for the workers. Such housing structures would normally be built so that their inhabitants would have easy access to the work site yet. Like many ancient dwelling c..."

title: Alchemist's Shop (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> This is the workplace of the ancient alchemist, home to secret potions and mysterious concoctions. In it, the earliest experiments in the sciences of chemistry and medicine occur, as man strives to discover cures and uncover answers to questions, or perhaps just produce a better-cleaning soap! But beware, all these arcane experiments can cause some pollution."

title: Drama (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> Alfred Hitchcock once said, "Drama is life with the dull bits cut out." If he'd been alive during ancient times, he might have uttered these same words when facing a play from Euripides. Reflecting the interesting (and often) tragic parts of "life" on the stage was an important part of the ancient world, and helped to shape our modern culture."

title: Ballistics (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> The engines of war (catapults, ballistas, trebuchets, etc.) played a vital role in ancient warfare. Laying siege to, and capturing, stoutly walled enemy cities were important -- not only to expand one’s land holdings, but to also spread one's culture."

title: Horsemanship (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> Skill in the saddle helped develop the powerful cavalry regiments of ancient man. The ability to tame and train horses for war is a difficult task that takes skill and patience, and the ancient cultures performed this duty splendidly."

title: Ship Building (Civ3)/Mesopotamia/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> Shipbuilding is an art form that ancient man developed early. Building vessels that could cross the “endless seas” of the ancient world was a paramount importance to the fledgling cultures that arose in the Mesopotamian and Mediterranean basins."

title: Architecture (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> Some of the greatest architects of the world lived during ancient times: the pyramid builders of Egypt, the parthenon builders of Greece, the colosseum builders of Rome. All of them shared a genius for geometry and physics, of form and function, and they created structures that have withstood the ravages of time."

comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> Sun Tzu noted, "War is a moral contest that is won in the temples before it is ever fought." This philosophy can be extended to include military training and preparedness. Very few are born to war, and fewer still are blessed with an inherent sense of tactics and strategy. So it is that the uneducated, undisciplined, and unruly warriors of the ancient world needed guidance and constant, constant drilling before th..."

title: Cuneiform (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> Cuneiform was the earliest form of writing in the Mesopotamian region. It originated as a picture language, similar to hieroglyphics, and with repeated use over time these pictures became simpler and then abstract. Eventually they developed into a form of syllabic alphabet which used wedge and hook shapes. The word cuneiform is derived from the Latin cuneus, which means wedge, and forma, which means shape. Most co..."

comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> A tribal council is a simple governmental organization wherein various groups or “tribes” of people (often sharing common cultural traits) select a person to represent their interests in a gathering of spokesmen from other tribes. These tribal representatives will often gather around large campfires or within structures such as teepees (i.e., Native Americans) and discuss issues and solve problems affecting th..."

title: Oligarchy (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> An oligarchy is a governmental organization wherein the power of the state has been usurped by a few citizens. The Roman government fell several times into an oligarchy; for example, under the decemvirs when they became the only magistrates in the commonwealth."

title: Diplomacy (advance) (Civ3)/Mesopotamia/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> Diplomacy in some form or another would have predated recorded history, in the form of hunting and marriage agreements between tribes. Diplomatic messengers were usually inviolable and would frequently carry some kind of emblem showing their "diplomatic" status. With the development of forms of writing these early diplomatic processes became more formalized. Not coincidentally, the earliest reliable evidence of di..."

During the Neolithic period as people started to settle into fixed agricultural communities this domestication intensified. Originally kept mainly for their meat, sheep and goats became valuable also for their milk and wool. Cattle were domesticated both for meat and skin and as work animals for agriculture;..."

Flint was one of the most popular stones for use as a tool, but fine sandstone and some volcanic rocks were also widely used. title: Sailing (Civ3)/Mesopotamia/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> The first sails were probably just a square sheet of animal skin hung from a horizontal pole, while later woven cloths were stretched between poles. While this does allow sailing there are several problems with these designs. title: Mining (Civ3)/Mesopotamia/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> There is evidence of surface mining dating back to prehistoric times. The first mining was probably for flints, which was used for knives, scrapers and arrowheads. The oldest known underground mine was in Swaziland over 40,000 years ago, to mine for ochre to use as a body pigment in ceremonies. During the Neolithic Age shafts were dug to extract flint from deeper in the earth. Gold, copper and silver were other mi..."

title: Irrigation (advance) (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> Irrigation is the artificial watering of land, usually for agriculture. The earliest use of irrigation was by the Egyptians along the Nile River around 5000 BC. Other Mesopotamian civilizations were using irrigation by around 2000 BC, as were the Chinese. Many different techniques of irrigation have been developed over time, including canals and ditches and mechanical devices to bail water from waterways to higher..."

title: Chariotry (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> Chariotry is believed to have originated in Mesopotamia around 3000 BC. The first four-wheeled chariots pulled by oxen were used to transport troops to the battle but they dismounted to fight. The later two-wheeled versions with a light spoked wheel and pulled by horses was considerably faster and more maneuverable than its predecessor. Spearmen and archers fighting "mounted" inside the chariot provided a superior..."

comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> When function and form coalesce, mighty cities are built. Many ancient cities were built from plans laid out long before the first pavement stones were laid. A gridwork of main streets running north and south and east and west, with a public square or forum in the center was a common feature in many ancient cities of Mesopotamia, such as Nineveh and Babylon. Ancient city planners worked diligently to design cities..."

title: Alchemy (Civ3)/Civilopedia
comment: Created page with "<noinclude>{{Civilopedia|Civilopedia (Civ3)}}</noinclude> Alchemy is an ancient science concerned with the changing of metal into gold, the discovery of a cure for all diseases, and the quest to prolong life, accepted by many as a precursor to modern medicine and other sciences. Over the ages, alchemists have toiled in their dark hovels for answers to the most important questions of our time."

title: Work Hours (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== Work hours represent the length of the workday for each worker. title: Veterans (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== When a military Unit survives a battle, it becomes a Veteran Unit. This status bestows a small bonus to the Unit's {{LinkCTP2|Attack}} capabilities.  [[Category:Game concepts (CTP2)]]"

title: Treaty (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== A leader that wishes to make a standing agreement with another empire can include a Treaty in their diplomatic proposal. title: Tile improvement (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== Tile Improvements serve several purposes. The cost of Tile Impro..."

comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== When a rival empire rejects or counters a {{LinkCTP2|Diplomatic}} proposal, a leader may find it necessary to Threaten them with action in order to force them to agree. comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== Terraforming is the process of converting one terrain type into another. As empires expand all over the world, the need for good land becomes dire. Fortunately, players can use {{LinkCTP2|Public Works}} resources to Terraform undesirable terrain tiles into more useful, more productive land. title: Support Cost (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== Waging war is not without its price. When a city builds a unit, the cost of that unit is measured in the {{LinkCTP2|Production}} resources it takes to build it. Once built, however, the unit incurs an additional cost of maintaining its health and training. This Military Support cost is extracted from the total {{LinkCTP2|Production}} output of an empire. The larger the military, the more..."

title: Stealth Units (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== Stealth Units are some of the more powerful units in Call To Power II. Primarily, any entity with normal vision (standard units, cities, listening posts) cannot see stealth units - they are only visible to each other. In addition, almost all Stealth Units have unconventional attacks. They can siphon {{LinkCTP2|Gold}}, interrupt {{LinkCTP2|Production}}, raise and lower {{LinkCTP2|Happines..."

title: Starvation (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== The more people there are in a {{LinkCTP2|City}}, the more {{LinkCTP2|Food}} the city must produce to feed them. For each turn a city fails to produce enough food, the city starves. Each city can endure a state of starvation for up to three turns. After three turns, the {{LinkCTP2|city size}} decreases by one.  Fortunately, there are three {{LinkCTP2|Improvements}} that increase a city's..."

title: Specialists (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== Specialists represent groups of citizens who are not primarily involved in the collection of resources. Rather, they can help boost certain specific resources in order to achieve a particular goal in the city. Each specialist is enabled by a specific {{LinkCTP2|Advance}} and will be unavailable the advance is discovered.  There are five types of specialists: Entertainers - enabled by {{L..."

title: Special Forces (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== Special Forces units are a subset of military units whose military readiness status is always "At War." In this way, they are always ready for battle, unaffected by global {{LinkCTP2|Military Readiness}} settings, incurring full support costs at all times.  [[Category:Game concepts (CTP2)]]"

title: Slave (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== Slaves are {{LinkCTP2|Workers}} who do not enjoy the benefit of citizenship. They are prisoners, in a sense, forced to work in a foreign city for no pay. Slaves only eat half of the {{LinkCTP2|Food}} of standard {{LinkCTP2|Workers}}.  An empire can only acquire slaves by sending {{LinkCTP2|Slavers}} on slave raids in neighboring empires. The act of enslaving others is seen as a grave off..."

title: Sea Colony (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== Built exclusively by {{LinkCTP2|Sea Engineer}} units, Sea Colonies are {{LinkCTP2|Cities}} on the floor of the ocean. They have all the same aspects of traditional land {{LinkCTP2|Cities}}, except they cannot build any pre-{{LinkCTP2|Modern Age}} {{LinkCTP2|Improvements}}.  [[Category:Game concepts (CTP2)]]"

title: Science Setting (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== The Science Setting represents the percentage of {{LinkCTP2|Commerce}} that is devoted to scientific research. The higher the setting, the better funded and more capable of discovery one's {{LinkCTP2|Scientists}} are. Each government type has a Maximum Science Setting that reflects that regime's dedication to the pursuit of technological and cultural advancement.  Category:Game concept..."

title: Science (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== In order to research {{LinkCTP2|Advances}}, an empire must generate {{LinkCTP2|Science}}. The most common way to do this is to devote a portion of the total {{LinkCTP2|Commercial}} output of one's empire to scientific research. Each city also can generate {{LinkCTP2|Science }}by turning {{LinkCTP2|Workers}} into {{LinkCTP2|Scientists}}, or building {{LinkCTP2|Improvements}} that boost Sc..."

title: Rush Buy (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== Although {{LinkCTP2|Cities}} build {{LinkCTP2|Units}}, {{LinkCTP2|Improvements}} and {{LinkCTP2|Wonders}} with available {{LinkCTP2|Production}} resources, a player may wish to speed up the build process by throwing money at it. title: Rivers (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== Rivers add value to the terrain through which they flow. They increase the amount of {{LinkCTP2|Food}}, {{LinkCTP2|Production}} and {{LinkCTP2|Commerce}} on a tile, and makes travel easier by reducing terrain-based movement costs.  [[Category:Game concepts (CTP2)]] [[Category:Terrain (CTP2)]]"

title: Riot (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== When {{LinkCTP2|Cities}} reach a certain level of unhappiness, outraged citizens take to the streets and riot. title: Revolution (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== Revolution causes a city to break free from their empire and form a completely new nation. title: Request (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== A Request is one of the three diplomatic options players have in formulating proposals.  Requests may involve asking for {{LinkCTP2|Gold}} or a {{LinkCTP2|City}}. They may be calls to honor agreements or reduce unconventional weapons arsenals. title: Regard (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== Regard is the worth and estimation that other empires hold for the player. comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== Rations are the amount of {{LinkCTP2|Food}} each citizen consumes per turn. comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== Players can use Public Works to build {{LinkCTP2|Tile Improvements}} and {{LinkCTP2|Terraform}} terrain. title: Production (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== Production is one of the three basic resources in Call To Power II. title: Population (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== Each city has a Population, representing the total number of citizens who live there. As a city's Population grows, so does it's productivity. With each increase in Population, another {{LinkCTP2|Worker}} adds to the resource-gathering potential of a city. A good leader can effectively manage Pollution on an Empire and City level. However, one must use {{LinkC..."

There are three military readiness states: At War, On Alert and At Peace.   When At War, all units are fully trained and ready to fight. They incur full support costs and have full health (until attacked). On Alert status has reduced support costs. Because of this, unit health..."

If the cost of {{LinkCTP2|Improvement}} maintenance in all {{LinkCTP2|Cities}} exceeds the amount of {{LinkCTP2|Gold}} in the treasury, {{LinkCTP2|Improve..."

With Infrastructure, the total {{LinkCTP2|Production}} output of the city is converted and..."

In their infancy, {{LinkCTP2|Cities}} are little more than a loose collection of dwellings. Improvements make the city more efficient and enable citizens to generate more {{LinkCTP2|Food}}, {{LinkCTP2|Commerce}} and {{LinkCTP2|Production}}. Improvements can also help reduce {{LinkCTP2|Crime}}, increase or decr..."

comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== Each city has an individual Happiness rating that indicates how satisfied citizens are with their lives. The empire-wide Happiness indicator reflects the general disposition of one's empire as a whole. Wise leaders will maintain the Happiness of their people by providing them with as much {{LinkCTP2|Food}}, as short a {{LinkCTP2|Workday}} and as high a {{LinkCTP2|Wage}} as possible. They..."

title: Growth (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== The Growth Rating indicates how quickly {{LinkCTP2|Cities}} increase their {{LinkCTP2|Population}}. Several factors contribute to the growth rate, including the distribution of labor in {{LinkCTP2|Cities}}, {{LinkCTP2|Improvements}} that promote growth and the {{LinkCTP2|Government}} type under which a leader rules his or her empire. Cities that produce an abundance of {{LinkCTP2|Food}}..."

title: Gold (currency) (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== Gold is the currency of Call to Power II, and one of the key resources in the game. It is used to speed up {{LinkCTP2|Unit}}, {{LinkCTP2|Improvement}} and {{LinkCTP2|Wonder}} production times by allowing the player to rush buy an item in the build queue.  The most common way to generate Gold in one's {{LinkCTP2|Cities}} is through Commerce. Like {{LinkCTP2|Food}} or {{LinkCTP2|Production..."

title: Fuel (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== All aerial units have a set amount of Fuel. When they move they consume one unit of Fuel per tile. If a unit remains in a tile without moving, it consumes one unit of fuel per turn. Aerial units must land on a {{LinkCTP2|City}}, {{LinkCTP2|Airbase}} or {{LinkCTP2|Aircraft Carrier}} before their Fuel runs out or they will crash.  [[Category:Game concepts (CTP2)]]"

title: Food (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== Food is one of the fundamental resources of the game. All {{LinkCTP2|Cities}} grow and harvest Food by working the tiles of land in and around the city. The city limits (represented by a white dotted line drawn on the map) indicate from which tiles a city draws Food. Different terrain types grow varying levels of Food, and {{LinkCTP2|Farm}} {{LinkCTP2|Tile Improvements}} can help a city..."

title: Empire Size (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== The size of one's empire, measured in the number of {{LinkCTP2|Cities}}, is only of concern when it comes to {{LinkCTP2|Government}} type. Not all {{LinkCTP2|Governments}} are adequate for large empires.  If a player's empire is too large for the current {{LinkCTP2|Government}} type, the citizens will become {{LinkCTP2|Unhappy}}. It is wise to switch {{LinkCTP2|Government}} types to one..."

title: Embargo (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== When a player embargoes a nation's {{LinkCTP2|trade}}, he or she is cutting off all trade relations with that nation. The embargoed nation is unable to create {{LinkCTP2|trade routes}} with the player's cities, which effectively prevents them from drawing any trade profits from them. In Call To Power II, players can use the {{LinkCTP2|threat}} of embargo as a {{LinkCTP2|diplomatic}} weap..."

title: Disband City (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== If, during the course of the game, a player wishes to remove a {{LinkCTP2|City}} from the map, he or she may disband it. The {{LinkCTP2|City}} may be in a poor location, vulnerable to attack or in some way unmanageable or undesirable. One can only disband a city of size 3 or less. Once disbanded, the {{LinkCTP2|City}} is eradicated and a {{LinkCTP2|Settler}} unit is created.  There is no..."

title: Diplomacy (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== Diplomacy is the art of negotiation. It is also one of the central foci of the game. Once a player makes contact with a foreign empire, he or she may engage in basic diplomatic relations. {{LinkCTP2|Establishing Embassies}} in foreign {{LinkCTP2|Cities}} open up more diplomatic options.  In Call To Power II, Diplomacy is conducted by sending proposals to other players. Players can compri..."

title: Defense (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== Every {{LinkCTP2|Unit}} has a Defense rating representing its ability to withstand an {{LinkCTP2|Attack}}. City Defenses can be augmented through such {{LinkCTP2|Improvements}} as {{LinkCTP2|City Walls}} and {{LinkCTP2|Forcefields}}.  [[Category:Game concepts (CTP2)]]"

title: Crime (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== When people feel that their needs are not met, they take matters into their own hands. If this {{LinkCTP2|Unhappiness}} reaches a certain level, the unfortunate by-product is criminal activity.   In Call To Power II, Crime creates reductions in {{LinkCTP2|Food}}, {{LinkCTP2|Commerce}} and {{LinkCTP2|Production}}, representing the "loss" of these basic elements to corruption and theft.  S..."

comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== Commerce is one of the basic resources of the game. Commerce represents the activity of buying, selling and trading goods and services in a city. It produces {{LinkCTP2|Gold}}, which pays for workers' {{LinkCTP2|Wages}} and funds {{LinkCTP2|Science}}. Players can also use accumulated {{LinkCTP2|Gold}} to {{LinkCTP2|Rush Buy}} {{LinkCTP2|Improvements}} and {{LinkCTP2|Wonders}}.  Commerce..."

title: City (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== Cities, and the management of them, are the prime focus of Call To Power II. With them, players can build {{LinkCTP2|Units}}, {{LinkCTP2|Improvements}} and Wonders. They draw the three main resources, {{LinkCTP2|Food}}, {{LinkCTP2|Production}} and {{LinkCTP2|Commerce}}, from the surrounding tiles. As the population of a city expands, so does its influence. Larger cities have more tiles f..."

title: Capitalization (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''. It converts {{LinkCTP2|Production}} to {{LinkCTP2|Gold}}.  ==Gameplay== Capitalization converts {{LinkCTP2|Production}} to {{LinkCTP2|Gold}}. A city that chooses Capitalization in its build queue turns all of its {{LinkCTP2|Production}} power into {{LinkCTP2|Gold}}. Capitalization remains in the build queue until the player changes it to something else.  [[Category:Game concepts (CTP2)]]"

title: Atrocity (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== Atrocities are events so abominable and horrifying, they provoke the anger and condemnation of the world community. In Call To Power II, certain special attacks, such as a {{LinkCTP2|Nuclear Attack}}, {{LinkCTP2|Nano-Attack}} or {{LinkCTP2|Nanite Cleansing}} constitute atrocities. Should a nation choose to engage in such nefarious warfare, they will assuredly find themselves having to an..."

title: Alliance (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== An Alliance is the supreme achievement of {{LinkCTP2|Diplomacy}} in Call To Power II, representing a strong bond between nations, molded through years of friendship, trust, and mutual {{LinkCTP2|Regard}} for one another.   The conditions for an Alliance are simple: Both nations must share a {{LinkCTP2|Peace Treaty}} and a Military Pact with each other. They must also have an extremely hi..."

title: Active Defense (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "'''{{CleanPageName}}''' is a game concept in ''[[Call to Power II]]''.  ==Gameplay== There are two types of Active Defense: Anti-Air and Anti-Naval. A unit with Active Defense automatically {{LinkCTP2|Bombards}} any Unit of a specific type that comes within range. Active Defense is a ranged attack, so the Unit does not put itself in danger when actively defending.  [[Category:Game concepts (CTP2)]]"

title: Refuel (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "When an air unit comes to rest on either an {{LinkCTP2|Airbase}} or a city with an {{LinkCTP2|Airport}}, it will Refuel the next turn. Refueling restores the unit's full movement range.  [[Category:Unit actions (CTP2)]]"

title: Ranged Attack (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "Units with '''ranged attack''' capability are ideal for supporting offensive and defensive units. Their ranged attack enables them to attack enemy targets from the rear line in battle. However, if there are no units to hold the front line, ranged units will be moved to fight at close quarters. Most ranged units are poorly equipped to fight this way, however, and should, as much as possible, be included with offensive and defensive units.  [[Category:Unit actions (CTP2)]]"

title: Nanite Cleansing (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "The most devastating attack in the game, the '''Nanite Cleansing''' attack totally annihilates any trace of humanity in the target area. It destroys the target city and all of its inhabitants, any improvements within the area of effect, as well as any units that happen to be within range.  This attack constitutes an {{LinkCTP2|Atrocity}}.  [[Category:Unit actions (CTP2)]]"

title: Assassinate ruler (CTP2)
comment: Changed redirect target from [[Assassinate ruler (CTP2)]] to [[Assassinate Ruler (CTP2)]]

title: Assassinate Ruler (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "{{LinkCTP2|Eco-Terrorist}}s can '''assassinate the ruler''' of another nation. If they succeed in the assassination, the target nation descends into {{LinkCTP2|Anarchy}}.  [[Category:Unit actions (CTP2)]]"

title: Nano-attack (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "The {{LinkCTP2|Eco-Terrorist}}'s main weapon, the '''Nano-Attack''' has a 30% of destroying each {{LinkCTP2|Improvement}} within the target city. Any city {{LinkCTP2|Trading}} with the target city has a 20% chance of being infected as well.  [[Category:Unit actions (CTP2)]]"

title: Plague (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "The most devastating biological weapons attack in the game, the '''Plague''' attack releases a highly contagious, extremely lethal supervirus into the air. Death comes quickly and painfully. The city's {{LinkCTP2|Population}} is decreased by 20%. Any city trading with the target city has a 30% chance of being infected as well.  This attack is considered an {{LinkCTP2|Atrocity}}.  [[Category:Unit actions (CTP2)]]"

title: Infect City (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "The Infector's primary attack releases a bio-weapons attack on unsuspecting citizens. This attack does not kill people. Rather, it makes a large percentage of the populace extremely ill. They are unhappy and unable to work for 5 turns. There is a sharp reduction in {{LinkCTP2|Happiness}} and {{LinkCTP2|Production}} as a result.  Any city trading with the target city has a 30% chance of being infected as well.  [[Category:Unit actions (CTP2)]]"

title: Clear Target (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "With the {{LinkCTP2|Target}} function, a player can designate enemy {{LinkCTP2|Cities}} as targets for {{LinkCTP2|Nuke}}s in the event of a nuclear attack. The '''Clear Target''' action enables the player to remove the {{LinkCTP2|Target}} designation from a {{LinkCTP2|Nuke}}, freeing it up for use elsewhere.  [[Category:Unit actions (CTP2)]]"

title: Target Nuke (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "The '''Target''' action enables leaders to set up a reciprocal attack system in the event of a surprise nuclear attack. When a player builds a {{LinkCTP2|Nuke}}, they can target that {{LinkCTP2|Nuke}} on an enemy city. If that enemy attacks the player with {{LinkCTP2|Nuke}}s, all nukes that have pre-designated Targets automatically launch. The Targeted {{LinkCTP2|Nuke}} must remain in a city and cannot be moved.  [[Category:Unit actions (CTP2)]]"

title: Sue (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "The '''Sue''' function has two purposes. {{LinkCTP2|Lawyer}}s can rid friendly {{LinkCTP2|Cities}} of enemy Franchises. {{LinkCTP2|Lawyer}}s can also Sue other {{LinkCTP2|Lawyer}} or {{LinkCTP2|Corporate Branch}} units to destroy them.  The attack costs 500 Gold to perform and always succeeds.  [[Category:Unit actions (CTP2)]]"

title: File Injunction (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "If a player wishes to stop an enemy city from building a certain item, say, a wonder or a particular unit, they can send in the suits. {{LinkCTP2|Lawyer}}s can '''File an Injunction''', which stops all {{LinkCTP2|Production}} in the city for one turn. This attack is always successful, but it does cost money to perform.  [[Category:Unit actions (CTP2)]]"

title: Advertise (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "{{LinkCTP2|Corporate Branch}}es can '''advertise''' in foreign {{LinkCTP2|Cities}}. They run ads for products that foreigners have no access to, heightening desire for material goods and causing people to be unhappy.  [[Category:Unit actions (CTP2)]]"

title: Franchise (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "{{LinkCTP2|Corporate Branch}}es can Establish a '''Franchise''' in an enemy city. If successful, the Franchise extracts 10% of the {{LinkCTP2|Production}} from that city and gives it to the attacking empire. This Production will be diverted not to cities, but to pay unit upkeep costs. If there is any left over after upkeep costs are paid, it will go into {{LinkCTP2|Public Works}}.  [[Category:Unit actions (CTP2)]]"

title: Free Slave (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "An {{LinkCTP2|Abolitionist}} unit can perform the '''free {{LinkCTP2|Slaves}}''' special attack. If successful, it frees one {{LinkCTP2|Slave}} from the target {{LinkCTP2|City}} and converts it to a citizen in the nearest friendly city.  [[Category:Unit actions (CTP2)]]"

title: Aid Uprising (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "The {{LinkCTP2|Abolitionist}} can '''aid a {{LinkCTP2|Slave}} Uprising''' in a foreign city that contains {{LinkCTP2|Slaves}}. If the attack is successful, the city will {{LinkCTP2|Revolt}} and become a new empire.  The cost of each attack depends on the distance from the nation's capitol and the number of {{LinkCTP2|Slaves}} in the city. The {{LinkCTP2|Slaves}} need not be the same nationality as the {{LinkCTP2|Abolitionist}} to {{LinkCTP2|Revolt}}.   Category:Unit ac..."

title: Capture Slaves (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "The {{LinkCTP2|Slaver's}} primary attack is '''capturing slaves'''. A successful attack reduces the target city's {{LinkCTP2|Population}} by 1 and places a {{LinkCTP2|Slave}} in one of the attacker's {{LinkCTP2|Cities}}.  [[Category:Unit actions (CTP2)]]"

title: Faith Healing (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "{{LinkCTP2|Televangelists}} bring the power of prayer to their services with '''Faith Healing'''. If this attack is successful, citizens in the target city will pay for the privilege of having their ailments cured, and the money will go to the {{LinkCTP2|Televangelist}}'s empire.  [[Category:Unit actions (CTP2)]]"

title: Sell Indulgence (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "{{LinkCTP2|Cleric}}s can '''sell indulgences''' in enemy {{LinkCTP2|Cities}}. This simultaneously makes people happy, and, like most religious attacks, generates cash.  This attack is always successful and costs nothing to perform. If the city is already converted to the attacker's religion, the attack generates more money.  [[Category:Unit actions (CTP2)]]"

title: Soothsay (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "People look to {{LinkCTP2|Cleric}}s for answers about the state of their lives and, more importantly, what the future has in store for them. A {{LinkCTP2|Cleric}} can Soothsay, preaching doom and damnation for the people of the target city. This sends people into a panic, and unhappiness takes a sharp dive for a turn.  This attack is always successful. It costs 500 {{LinkCTP2|Gold}} to perform.  [[Category:Unit actions (CTP2)]]"

title: Convert City (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "Clerics and Televangelists swoop into town with their message of faith and redemption, and can '''convert''' a foreign city to their religion. The grateful citizens jubilantly shower the prophets with money. Televangelists are considerably more effective (and profitable) than Clerics, especially in {{LinkCTP2|Cities}} with {{LinkCTP2|Television}}s.  [[Category:Unit actions (CTP2)]]"

title: Plant Nuke (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "The ability to '''plant nukes''' in enemy {{LinkCTP2|Cities}} is the most nefarious and powerful act a {{LinkCTP2|Spy}} or {{LinkCTP2|Cyber Ninja}} can perform. There is a 25% chance of success for the Spy, and a 35% chance of success for the Cyber Ninja. The risk of capture is significant - 75% for the Spy and 50% for the Cyber Ninja.  If the attack is successful, the nuke detonates, destroying the target city and all Tile Improvements within three tiles of the city. As..."

title: Incite Revolution (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "The {{LinkCTP2|Spy}} and {{LinkCTP2|Cyber Ninja}} can infiltrate an enemy city and '''incite''' the citizens to revolt. If the attack is successful, the city forms a new empire. The {{LinkCTP2|Spy}} has a 25% chance of success, with a 50% chance of getting caught. The {{LinkCTP2|Cyber Ninja}} has a 35% chance of success, with a 25% chance of getting caught. If either unit is caught, they are killed.  This attack costs {{LinkCTP2|Gold}} to perform. The total cost of the a..."

title: Steal Advance (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "{{LinkCTP2|Spies}} or {{LinkCTP2|Cyber Ninjas}} can attempt to '''Steal an {{LinkCTP2|Advance}}''' from a rival empire. The chances of success are 35% for the {{LinkCTP2|Spy}} and 50% for the {{LinkCTP2|Cyber Ninja}}. If successful, the attacker gains the {{LinkCTP2|Advance}} immediately, including any new building options. There is a 50% that the {{LinkCTP2|Spy}} will be captured and killed. The {{LinkCTP2|Cyber Ninja}}'s chances of capture are 25%.  Category:Unit act..."

title: Spy (concept) (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "One of the more powerful attacks of the {{LinkCTP2|Spy}} and {{LinkCTP2|Cyber Ninja}} is the '''spy''' attack. If successful, the {{LinkCTP2|Spy}} attack reveals everything about the city - what is being built, how many people live there, how many military units are garrisoned, how much {{LinkCTP2|Food}}, {{LinkCTP2|Gold}} and {{LinkCTP2|Production}} are produced.  This information is vital for preparing to attack a city. However, {{LinkCTP2|Spies}} and {{LinkCTP2|Cyber..."

title: Hold Reception (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "Dignitaries visiting foreign {{LinkCTP2|Cities}} often find an occasion to wine and dine the heads of state that host them. They use this opportunity to curry favor with the host nation and "grease the wheels" of {{LinkCTP2|Diplomacy}}. The {{LinkCTP2|Diplomat}} and {{LinkCTP2|Empathic Diplomat}} that use the '''Hold Reception''' action increase the host nation's diplomatic {{LinkCTP2|Regard}}.  Each subsequent Reception held has a lesser effect.  Category:Unit actions..."

title: Establish Embassy (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "{{LinkCTP2|Diplomats}} and {{LinkCTP2|Empathic Diplomats}} share the ability to '''Establish an Embassy''' in a foreign city. Without Embassies, only the most basic of diplomatic options are available to the player. Embassies enable high-level {{LinkCTP2|Diplomacy}} to take place. They are crucial for cementing good relations with foreign nations.  [[Category:Unit actions (CTP2)]]"

title: Settle (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "The three "settler" units in the game - the {{LinkCTP2|Settler}}, {{LinkCTP2|Urban Planner}} and {{LinkCTP2|Sea Engineer}} are the only units with the '''settle''' function.  {{LinkCTP2|Settlers}} can build {{LinkCTP2|Cities}} of {{LinkCTP2|Population}} size 1 on any land tile. {{LinkCTP2|Urban Planners}} build {{LinkCTP2|Cities}} of {{LinkCTP2|Population}} size 1, with several building {{LinkCTP2|Improvements}} constructed, on land tiles as well. The {{LinkCTP2|Sea Engi..."

title: Space Launch (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "Space Planes can perform sub-orbital launches with the Launch command. In order to do this, load a {{LinkCTP2|Space Plane}} with cargo and Launch. The unit can touch down in any friendly city on the map within 3 turns.  [[Category:Unit actions (CTP2)]]"

title: Disband (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "A player may want to '''Disband''' a unit for a variety of reasons. Older and obsolete units are often too weak to be much of an asset in combat. Some units have specific functions and, once successful in their mission,   If a player disbands a unit in one of his or her {{LinkCTP2|Cities}}, half of the unit's original {{LinkCTP2|Slave}} cost will contribute to the current build queue in that city. Units Disbanded in the field simply disappear.  Category:Unit actions (C..."

title: Unload (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "{{LinkCTP2|Transport}} units may use the '''unload''' command to move their cargo onto an adjacent tile. Only {{LinkCTP2|Marines}} can be unloaded onto enemy-occupied tiles. Otherwise, the tile must be unoccupied.  [[Category:Unit actions (CTP2)]]"

title: Load (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "A Transport unit is one that can carry and unload other land-based units. Naval transports, such as carracks and troop ships can Transport land units across the ocean. Air Transports, such as the {{LinkCTP2|Cargo Helicopter}} and {{LinkCTP2|Space Plane}}, Transport land units across any terrain.  If a Transport unit is destroyed in an attack, all of the units in its cargo are destroyed as well.  [[Category:Unit actions (CTP2)]]"

title: Bombard (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "The '''Bombard''' attack is a type of long distance attack. Units can Bombard {{LinkCTP2|Cities}} and either destroy improvements, kill fortified units or reduce the city's population. Units can also bombard other units, damaging the enemy unit without risk. A unit cannot move after bombarding.  Not all bombarding units have the range or capability to bombard every kind of target. {{LinkCTP2|Catapult}}s, for instance, can bombard any land unit or city, but cannot bombard..."

title: Reform City (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "The '''reform city''' function can only be used on a city in one's own empire. Should a city fall prey to a cleric or televangelist's {{LinkCTP2|conversion}}, any military unit can reform the city. The city is unhappy for one turn because of the reformation.  [[Category:Unit actions (CTP2)]]"

title: Expel (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "Leaders who wish to remove an enemy {{LinkCTP2|Stealth Unit}} (such as a {{LinkCTP2|Diplomat}}, {{LinkCTP2|Slaver}} or {{LinkCTP2|Lawyer}}) or non-military unit (such as a {{LinkCTP2|Settler}}, {{LinkCTP2|Urban Planner}} or {{LinkCTP2|Sea Engineer}}) from their own territory without attacking it (and thus angering one's rivals) can opt to Expel the unwanted unit. The Expelled unit takes no damage. It is simply moved to the nearest friendly city. This action does not affe..."

title: Piracy (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "Any unit can '''Pirate''' a trade route by standing over the route and selecting the Pirate option. When successful, the attacker does not destroy the route. Rather, it hijacks the {{LinkCTP2|Trade}} profits from that particular route for one turn. Piracy is considered an act of aggression and most certainly has {{LinkCTP2|Diplomatic}} consequences.  [[Category:Unit actions (CTP2)]]"

title: Pillage (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "Any land-based military unit can '''Pillage''' a tile. The act of Pillaging destroys any {{LinkCTP2|Tile Improvements}} on the tile. The success rate is 100%.  This act is an attack like any other, and will be considered an act of aggression by other nations.   [[Category:Unit actions (CTP2)]]"

title: Sentinel (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "The '''Sentinel''' function is available to every {{LinkCTP2|Unit}}. When a unit is in Sentinel Mode, it is removed from the cycle of units selected every turn. A Sentinel Unit is grayed out and remains so until one of the following occurs: *the Sentinel Unit is attacked *an enemy unit comes within visual range of the Sentinel Unit *the player clicks on the Unit  The Sentinel function is particularly useful when a player does not want to keep cycling through inactive uni..."

title: Fortify (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "Most land-based military units can '''Fortify''' on a tile for a {{LinkCTP2|Defense}} bonus. The Fortification process takes a few turns to complete. Once a unit is fortified (a small wall around the unit, similar to the Fortification {{LinkCTP2|Tile Improvement}}, indicates that the unit is Fortified) it enjoys an additional {{LinkCTP2|Defense}} bonus beyond any given by the terrain.  [[Category:Unit actions (CTP2)]]"

title: Assault (CTP2)
comment: Created page with "A unit may '''attack''' another unit by simply moving on to the tile the target unit occupies. The success of the attack depends on the relative strength of the attacker versus the defender, taking into account terrain bonuses, attack, defense and armor ratings.  [[Category:Unit actions (CTP2)]]"
